Fixed-checkpoint ablation and retrained comparison answer different questions. Adding/removing a transition-graph residual while holding backbone weights fixed measures that branch’s incremental utility for the particular checkpoint. It does not establish whether training with the branch improves the architecture: the backbone and residual may co-adapt. A directly relevant study uses frozen-backbone neighborhood score augmentation specifically to isolate post-training signal utility ([Lee and Ahn](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/16/19/9947)). Architectural benefit therefore requires separately trained baseline and graph models under matched data, tuning budgets, seeds, and validation candidates; checkpoint ablation remains a complementary diagnostic.

Cross-fitting constructs training features without the target example’s contribution. In graph stacking, out-of-fold predictions address feature leakage and training–inference mismatch caused by overfit base predictions ([BestowGNN](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=LO02YHxrxd)). Applied to transition graphs, the methodological implication is to exclude each training user’s entire history when constructing that user’s graph features, rather than removing only one target transition. However, replacing these user-excluding graphs with a full training graph at deployment can change edge support, normalization, sparsity, and residual-score scale; cross-fitting does not automatically eliminate this shift. Measure those differences and compare graph-construction policies using the same validation protocol. Keep validation targets out of graph construction and preserve the benchmark’s pinned splits: recommendation research shows unavailable-interaction leakage can change model rankings ([Ji et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11060)). These graph-specific recommendations are methodological inferences, not established results for this RecHarness task.
